In one word - inevitable.

We're already seeing on a daily basis the effects of increasing worker productivity, increasing automation, and overall increasing production efficiency. And this trend is only going to accelerate as we start to see more fields experience greater and greater levels of automation. Yet these massively streamlined production systems are worthless without people to purchase their product. You end up in a situation where companies need lots of people to buy stuff, yet reduced job availability and wages preclude that. UBI fixes this while also staying within a completely meritocratic system. Those of merit can and will do extremely well. Those of no merit will be able to live modest but comfortable lives. The only real downside is worker disincentive, but in a system where unemployment starts reaching dangerous levels this would no longer be an issue.

It would also have some great effects on the market. For instance you'd no longer need a minimum wage. When workers can afford to say no, the asymmetry of power in hiring would be gone. So we'd actually see the free market decide on worker compensation in a fair fashion, which is a great thing for everybody. The all but complete elimination of petty need based crime would be another perk. It'd also actually allow people to 'pull themselves up by their bootstraps' as the saying goes. Right now the vast majority of the vast majority of most peoples' income is gone the day they receive - rent, utilities, food, insurances, bills, and you're left with a small fraction of your paycheck. With your basic necessities covered, 100% of what you earn goes to you. That means even low paying jobs can provide a large effective utility in terms of improving quality of life. This paired with the free market wage levels would lead to very interesting results.

I agree. I would also like to add that there are many proposed methods of implementation that avoid the association with 'welfare' programs. For instance, economist Louis Kelso, inventor of the Employee Stock Ownership Program, proposed the realization of UBI through the creation of a kind of national mutual fund created by what was dubbed the Capital Homesteading Act. This avoided problems like the market adjustment to scheduled stipends which plagues low-income communities today. (the common phenomenon of stores and businesses in poor neighborhoods raising their prices around the same time of the month welfare and food stamps are distributed)

Many proponents of UBI in the past have seen UBI in a similar context of a kind of societal dividend owed on the national commons. In other words, industrial activity is rooted in the development of natural resources facilitated by taxpayer-built infrastructures which thus represent a national commons owned equally by all citizens. And thus we are logically owed, each individually, a dividend on that development like any other investor with the right to personally choose how that dividend is spent instead of it being pooled and spent by the government.

It still amazes me to see UBI being discussed openly in the US today. This is something I never thought I would see in my lifetime.

I was thinking about a spin on the idea of national commons previously. It would be interesting if all land was considered public - not as in owned by the government but owned by the people. The way you obtain land is simply by renting it from the public at a price determined in an open market exchange. This would be a radical transformation in society, but one that seems clearly for better if it could work. However, there is one major problem I can't see any solution to. That problem being development - this system would punish people who develop their land since the market price, and thus the price they will need to pay to retain the land, would go up. Logically this makes sense, but I think emotionally it'd feel atrocious living in a system where, for instance, fixing up a fixer upper suddenly means your 'rent' goes up.

This is similar to the concepts of Georgism or Geoism. The problem you note is rooted in the cultural delusion at the heart of real estate; that architecture is permanent and 'improves' property. Nothing really improves land, save the creation of utilities infrastructures. No structure you build on land can ever be truly permanent, just more and less difficult to remove and thus more-or-less damaging to the land. Look at those suggestions by themselves and they make no sense. They made a kind of sense in feudal times when lords were granted or bought titles to large tracts of land and the control and exploitation of serfs living on it. You could generally 'improve' the productivity of land by cultivating it, clearing forests, pulling out rocks, building irrigation, making granaries and mills, and otherwise creating this agricultural production infrastructure. But by pretending these things are reality today, even on the scale of houses, we've created the ponzi scheme of real estate. You build or renovate almost anything on land and its value automatically goes up about 20% over the cost of whatever you build. Buy a $30k plot of land, put $70k into building a house on it, you automatically have a roughly $120k property you can sell. Why? How? It's just a convention--like the looser convention of normal retail markup being around 30%--yet the basis of development and real estate investment. In real estate investment you don't make money on rents because that's taxable income. You make money on the refinance of property as value climbs, as the proceeds from loans isn't taxable. There's no logic or basis for this in reality. Everybody just plays the game.

In Japan property law keeps building and land values separate. Modest buildings like houses are considered to have no intrinsic value. They're furniture. Doesn't matter whether or not you have to take out loans to have something built. That debt doesn't automatically carry over to whoever subsequently buys the property--the house isn't part of the land. People don't treat houses like a life-long investment and repository of family wealth. And this idea makes sense when you consider the history there. There has traditionally been so many ways for homes to be destroyed in Japan--earthquakes, typhoons, tsunamis, volcanoes, runaway urban fires, war (periodic trampling by kaiju and giant robots...)--that the notion they could be permanent was plainly ridiculous. This is why the Japanese were the first to invent modular building systems for housing--the 'ken' system deriving from the size of the tatami mat--and standardized pre-cut lumber. They had to be able to recover from disasters quickly. And their traditional home interior designs reflected this. Everything important was designed to be picked up and moved at a moment's notice. Large towns had these armored underground or earth covered community vaults. When a big fire started, people would pick up and bring all their stuff to the vault.

There are downsides to this, of course. Fewer people own homes and often don't own the land they're on. Property doesn't change hands as frequently. Apartment buildings are more spartan and rents higher because their owners have to seek profit on rent instead of periodic refinance. Older homes and buildings tend to get run-down because, if you're planning to sell property, there's no incentive for up-keep. Homes and buildings are more-often demolished rather than renovated or repurposed. On the plus side, runaway gentrification and house flipping rackets don't happen, housebuilding is generally very efficient and refined in technique with homebuilding times a fraction of that elsewhere, and people don't have a perpetual bug up their ass about what kind of houses their neighbors build or what they do on their own property because it doesn't matter to the regional property values. So upper-middle-class people experiment and frequently rebuild their homes whole for the sake of new design trends. Japan has the most wildly creative and experimental housing in the world. Most every new idea or technology that comes along is embraced and explored. Modernism and Post-Modernism both flourish there. The Cult of Zoning never took hold there so there's much creativity in how property is used. People will do things like build homes on tiny weirdly shaped bits of land or build an automated vertical parking garage and use it to pay for a house on the top floor. And this is why Japan so often looks like the future (in the full spectrum from dystopian to utopian) while the US is forever reiterating a suburban lowest common denominator aesthetic, cultivating a dystopian banality and sameness to suburbia everywhere because it suits the finance industry and the modern need of wealth to be easily fungible. If you treat housing as a repository of wealth it's logically going to end up looking the same like money because its primary function is its fungibility, which means always conforming to the lowest-common-denominator in public taste.

Another concept of Louis Keslo's that complimented the Capital Homesteading Act was the Community Investment Corporation or Land-Home Bank. The basic idea was that, if you were doing a large development--like Buckminster Fuller's proposed Old Man River City project that Kelso was once involved with--you would create this corporation that held and developed all the land and the residents of the community you were building would buy the rights to the use of space for homes by buying shares of stock in the CIC. And you would get a dividend on these shares because a lot of the development would, naturally, be done for commercial purposes, leasing space to businesses. As the community grew, the value of these shares would grow, and their dividend would approach a UBI by retirement age. And so you had this option of helping the poor get access to property by giving them loans of shares that would be self-liquidating by their own dividends, the premise of this being that by living in the community, working at and patronizing its businesses, people are contributing to the growth in value and dividends of the CIC shares and thus paying their loan that way.
